articles.title: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled - PressReader
articles.summary: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled  PressReader
articles.full_text:
It’s been a year since a ceasefire deal brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump and Arab allies promised to end the war in Gaza, and Israel is still launching deadly strikes on the devastated territory. The agreement halted major military operations, freed all remaining hostages and increased humanitarian access. But it has failed to deliver on promises of a new Palestinian administration aided by international forces, the disarmament of Hamas and an end to Israel’s control over more than half the territory. Almost nothing has been rebuilt. Israel has tied any progress on the other issues to Hamas’ complete disarmament, while the militant group — and the Trump administration — say they should happen simultaneously. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hardened his stance over the summer, openly defying Trump, his most important ally, ahead of Israeli elections later this month.
The wrangling has left Gaza’s 2 million Palestinians in limbo. Most are sheltering in rodent-infested tent camps, the rubble of their former neighborhoods or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
In the Jabaliya area of the northern Gaza Strip, Abdullah Abu Zubaida’s family lives in a makeshift shelter built from the debris of their house.
“When the ceasefire began last October, we expected the war to halt, assassinations to cease, and aid to flow in,” he said. None of that has happened.
For Ne’man Abu Jarad and his family, displaced from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza to Khan Younis in the south, the truce also has brought no clear path home. The family, including five daughters, continues to live in tents.
“The ceasefire is merely nominal, ink on paper,” Abu Jarad said.
Early success raised hopes of ending the war
The 20-point ceasefire agreement, reached after months of negotiations under the Biden and Trump administrations, ended major military operations and led to the return of all the remaining hostages taken in Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack that ignited the war.
Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people that day and abducted 251. Israel responded with massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
After the deal was announced, Trump called for a new era of harmony in the Middle East. “We have a once-in-a-lifetime chance to put the old feuds and bitter hatreds behind us,” he said at a summit marking the deal.
The agreement called for much more
The agreement called for Hamas to hand over power to a committee of Palestinian administrators vetted by the Board of Peace, a new body chaired by Trump and charged with implementing the ceasefire.
The militants officially dissolved their government in July but left the civil ser-*
vice intact and remain the dominant power in the roughly 40% of Gaza not controlled by the Israeli military. Israel has meanwhile barred the new Palestinian administration from entering Gaza via Egypt.
The formation of an International Stabilization Force was announced in February but has yet to materialize. Indonesia, which pledged the largest troop contingent — 8,000 soldiers — put those plans on hold last spring as the world’s focus shifted to the Iran war.
Israel was supposed to withdraw from Gaza but has instead seized more territory, pushing the so-called yellow Line of Control westward toward the Mediterranean Sea. It has also carried out regular strikes on individuals it accused of violating the ceasefire, approaching the yellow line or having taken part in the Oct. 7 attack — strikes that have often killed civilians.
Israeli strikes have killed over 1,400 Palestinians since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.
More deadlock after Netanyahu defied Trump
In July, Trump announced a deal to disarm Hamas, portraying it as a breakthrough in the long-stalled process.
That deal, an extension of the original ceasefire, called for Hamas to disarm “in a gradual, sequential and time-bound manner” that is “linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases.” Hamas confirmed for the first time that it had agreed to disarm, also linking it to Israel halting its strikes and withdrawing from Gaza.
Days later, Netanyahu announced that Israel would not withdraw from any part of Gaza until after Hamas has been completely disarmed, explicitly rejecting the agreement announced by Trump.
The rare instance of friction between the two allies came as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his nationalist base ahead of Oct. 27 elections that could end his nearly unbroken 17-year rule, the longest in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu has come under fire over security and intelligence failures leading up to the Oct. 7 attack, with opponents accusing him of having been soft on Hamas. That gives him little space to make even minor compromises on Gaza, at least until a new government is formed, which could take months.
In the meantime, virtually nothing has been rebuilt in Gaza, Hamas is weakened but still in power, and a return to fighting cannot be ruled out.

articles.summary: Exclusive: Romania president calls for NATO oversight in the Black Sea  Euronews.comDrone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO’s response  AP NewsPutin brings war into Nato’s waters  The TelegraphBulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister  ReutersRussia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test  The Kyiv Independent
articles.full_text:
In an interview with Euronews, Romanian President Nicușor Dan warns that Black Sea security is under growing pressure as drone attacks hit commercial vessels off Romania and Bulgaria.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has said the Black Sea would only become safe after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends, as he called for greater NATO oversight in the region following drone strikes on commercial vessels in an interview with Euronews.
“I’m very optimistic that we’ll have the support and the capabilities in order to be better protected, because it’s an important economic question for Ukraine and for the whole region,” he said on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels held Friday.
The Romanian leader said frequent drone incursions into his country’s territory had begun roughly a year and a half ago, and that Bucharest had been “not prepared”. The country now faces a similar lack of preparedness to its east, Dan said.
“At the Black Sea, we are in the same situation,” he said, adding: “We have to protect the water under our territory.”
He also expressed confidence in continued support from US President Donald Trump, both for security in the Black Sea and for Romania’s position within the NATO military alliance.
“On defence, I think it’s a mutual benefit between us because we have an excellent position to project force towards other parts of the world,” Dan said.
The confidence comes amid bellicose statements from US President Donald Trump regarding Ukrainian and European security, such as troop cuts and a force posture review.
The president was in the Belgian capital for a quarterly summit attended by EU heads of state to discuss support for Ukraine, the bloc’s long-term budget and its growing trade deficit with China.
However, the increasingly hostile security situation in the Black Sea pushed the Romanian leader and his Bulgarian counterpart, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, to bring security threats higher up the agenda.
Dan told reporters after the summit that France had pledged “necessary equipment” and to “better understand our specific requirements in the Black Sea”.
“There are always new challenges, but fortunately, Romania has allies,” he said.
The escalating situation also prompted a meeting between the two leaders and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte to discuss stronger support. Bulgaria requested combat aircraft and anti-drone systems during the talks.
Rutte said afterwards that NATO would continue to strengthen its posture along the eastern flank, including by expanding its counter-drone capabilities.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he said in a statement on the social media platform X.
Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian ports along the Black Sea and the Danube River, leaving the war-torn country dependent on alternative routes to sell its grain to African and Middle Eastern markets.
However, this has exposed Europe’s shipping lanes to attacks.
Drones have damaged commercial vessels in the Black Sea off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania for three consecutive days leading up to the meeting in Brussels, as well as during the previous week. At least one vessel sank after being attacked by drones last week, killing two seafarers.
Neither Sofia nor Bucharest has definitively blamed Russia for the attacks. However, Radev told reporters earlier in the week that “logic” would suggest the Kremlin stood to benefit from the deadly incursions.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it,” he said.
Investigations into all the incidents are ongoing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference after meeting European leaders on Thursday that “you do not need a ground war for an invasion to occur”.
He added that Russia was testing Europe’s response to the attacks, referring to incidents in the Black Sea as well as an explosive-laden drone found at an airport in Leipzig.
“Violating another country's airspace is already an incursion,” Zelenskyy said.
“We have seen drones cross airspace and borders in Romania, Poland and Germany. A corresponding drone was found in Germany, by the way. Moldova and Bulgaria have also been affected. A great deal is happening today.”
Zelenskyy and other senior Ukrainian officials have publicly blamed Russia for some of these incidents, most notably a deadly drone attack that struck a vessel carrying Ukrainian grain off the Bulgarian coast.

articles.title: EU summit in Brussels: European powers intensify war drive against Russia - World Socialist Web Site
articles.summary: EU summit in Brussels: European powers intensify war drive against Russia  World Socialist Web Site
articles.full_text:
The EU summit held on Thursday and Friday in Brussels was an expression of the dangerous escalation of the international war crisis. While the Trump administration, amid its conflict with the European powers, is seeking at least for the moment a certain accommodation with Russia, the EU governments, led by Berlin, are pressing for the continuation and expansion of the Ukraine war. They want to shoulder an increasing share of the financial and military burdens themselves and build Europe into an independent military power.
This is accompanied by an escalation that threatens to provoke a direct war between NATO and Russia, including nuclear war. At the same time, the summit discussions on rearmament, “competitiveness,” trade war and migration underscore that the war drive abroad is inseparably linked to intensified social attacks and authoritarian measures at home.
Conflicts between Washington and Europe
At the center of the summit was the demonstrative support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Following an agreement with Putin on Russian diesel supplies, Trump had eased sanctions and criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He also demanded a change in Ukraine’s leadership. The European governments, by contrast, are determined to continue attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure and tighten sanctions.
European Council President António Costa declared on Friday, standing alongside Zelensky: “Now is not the time to withdraw support for Ukraine. Now is not the time to ease sanctions against Russia.” Instead, the EU must increase its support and pressure on Russia. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced preparations for a 22nd package of sanctions.
The German government is taking a particularly aggressive stance. Chancellor Friedrich Merz declared that the EU must “once again ... increase” its funding for Kiev in order to “provide lasting support” to Ukraine. This was necessary, he said, to defend “the political order of Europe.” The conflict with Washington now also concerns control over approximately €210 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets in Europe. According to reports, US negotiators want to use part of these assets in negotiations with Moscow. Merz brusquely rejected this: “That is our affair, and we will decide on it.”
Behind these differences lie rival geostrategic and economic interests. The European powers fear that Trump could conclude an agreement with Putin that would undermine their own war aims and influence in Eastern Europe. At the same time, Ukraine’s war effort remains dependent on American military technology and intelligence support. Reports of restrictions on the satellite-based Starshield system demonstrate this dependence particularly starkly.
Ever more billions for war
Zelensky put Ukraine’s war costs for 2027 at €155 billion and demanded at least €70 billion in additional European support. With this money, Ukraine could produce two to three times as many drones and massively increase military pressure on Russia. The EU has already set in motion a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027. No decision was reached in Brussels on the new demands for billions; the Commission has been tasked with developing financing options.
The scale of the sums already mobilized is enormous. According to a study by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, the German government puts its Ukraine support to date, including commitments, at around €100 billion. Approximately €41.7 billion is recorded as direct aid to Ukraine, while another €22 billion consists of future military commitments and possible expenditures. Together, this amounts to €63.7 billion, of which approximately €56.3 billion is military aid. In addition, €35.9 billion has been spent predominantly on Ukrainian refugees in Germany. Not all of the budgeted funds recorded have yet been disbursed.
The political thrust of the Kiel study is revealing. Under a headline emphasizing that “only” €41.7 billion actually went to Ukraine, it stresses that spending on refugees does “not support the Ukrainian government in its defense.” This juxtaposition alone makes the political orientation clear: While support for refugees and other social expenditures face growing pressure for cuts, ever larger sums are to be mobilized for the war effort. Added to this are hundreds of billions more that are to flow into military budgets in the coming years.
Concrete preparations for a NATO-Russia war
Parallel to the summit, the military confrontation is intensifying. NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich presented his “Theory of Victory” in Warsaw: “Block, Blunt, Break.” A potential attack is first to be repelled, then the opposing armed forces smashed, and finally the command, supply and production structures supporting them disabled. Grynkewich describes the strategy as defensive, but in a major war the planned operations could extend deep into Russian territory. He praised Germany as the “engine of NATO.”
At the same time, NATO conducted the nuclear war exercise “Steadfast Noon” in Italy this week, involving 17 countries, including German Tornado fighter jets. NATO describes it as a routine exercise without live nuclear weapons. Yet it rehearsed procedures for nuclear operations at a time when the risks of escalation are rapidly increasing.
Russia is responding to NATO’s constant provocations with nuclear threats. In early October, Putin warned that Russia could use its entire arsenal in the event of a blockade of Kaliningrad. Now, State Duma Deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov has told Lenta.ru that, in the event of a NATO attack, Russian nuclear strikes could target NATO headquarters, as well as US nuclear weapons bases in Germany, Belgium, Italy and Turkey. Zhuravlyov’s threat is not an official government statement. His remarks nevertheless demonstrate how concretely sections of the Russian establishment are discussing nuclear war in Europe.
Russian military commentators warn that NATO’s strategy could serve as a cover for “preemptive” strikes. They draw parallels to Hitler’s war of annihilation against the Soviet Union, which Nazi propaganda likewise justified as “defense” against an allegedly planned Soviet attack.
Regardless of NATO’s specific timetable for war, the mutual threats already demonstrate that an escalation could rapidly spiral out of control. In the Black Sea, Romania and Bulgaria are demanding additional NATO measures against Russia following drone attacks on merchant ships.
Rearmament and social devastation
Europe’s response to the war and the crisis of its alliance with Washington is a gigantic rearmament program. “ReArm Europe” is intended to make possible up to €800 billion in additional defense spending by 2030, while the SAFE program provides €150 billion in loans. In Germany, defense spending is to rise to approximately €140 billion in 2027—and to well over €200 billion in 2029. The German government wants to build the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional army.
These sums have immediate social consequences. While debt rules are relaxed for rearmament, European governments are organizing historic cuts to social benefits and public services. Under the slogan of “competitiveness,” the EU summit adopted measures for deregulation, accelerated approval procedures and further economic restructuring. Jobs are being eliminated on a massive scale, wages cut and working conditions worsened.
The EU also wants to create new trade policy instruments to take tougher action, particularly against China. Merz stated that the Commission had been given a mandate to this end. Von der Leyen announced additional import restrictions.
The migration debate at the summit also revealed its reactionary direction. Italy, Denmark and Poland attacked Spain’s planned legalization of the residence status of around 600,000 migrants. Discussions included tightening detention provisions in border procedures and suspending asylum applications in times of crisis. In the Middle East, against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran, the summit focused above all on securing trade and energy routes.
As the EU advances its global war offensive and reactionary domestic agenda, tensions among the European imperialist powers are growing. The dispute over the next EU budget for 2028 to 2034 exposed these rivalries. Net contributors, such as Sweden, are refusing the higher contributions being demanded, while the EU seeks to mobilize additional funds for strategic and military projects. No agreement has yet been reached.
The extreme escalation of war is also a response to growing social and political opposition in Europe. In France, Spain and other countries, mass protests and strikes are developing against social cuts, militarism and authoritarian measures. Confronted with the deep crisis of the established parties, the ruling classes are attempting to divert this opposition outward through war propaganda and nationalism and force the population to rally behind their war policies.
But this course will only further intensify social antagonisms. The gigantic military expenditures, the destruction of jobs and social benefits, and the increasing attacks on democratic rights will not extinguish the resistance of the working class and youth but further fuel it. At the same time, the escalating confrontation with Russia threatens to plunge all of Europe into a nuclear world war.
The decisive task is to arm the growing opposition with an independent socialist perspective. The working class must organize independently of the established parties and unite its struggles across all national borders against capitalism, militarism and war. The nationalist and militarist project of the European governments must be opposed with the struggle for the United Socialist States of Europe.

articles.title: UN Security Council Straw Poll Leaves Grynspan, Grossi, Rodrigues Birkett Without Five-Power Support - NewsCord
articles.summary: UN Security Council Straw Poll Leaves Grynspan, Grossi, Rodrigues Birkett Without Five-Power Support  NewsCord
articles.full_text:
UN chief race deadlocked
The UN Security Council held a straw poll on Friday and showed that none of the seven candidates for the next UN secretary-general has the support of all five permanent members with veto power, leaving the door open for new candidates. The process left Rebeca Grynspan, Rafael Grossi, and Guyana’s U.N. ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett as the three leading candidates, with each receiving two red “discourage” votes, while Grynspan remained at the top with nine “encourage” votes. The vote used red ballots to distinguish votes from the five powers, and the 15 council members voted to “encourage” or “discourage” the seven candidates or express “no opinion” in a secret poll.
Mike Waltz told reporters as he left the closed council meeting that the UN needs “strong, energetic leadership” to take the 193-member world body back to peace and security. The selection race also faced pressure to pick a woman, and Waltz said, “Of course, if the best candidate is a woman, we would welcome that.”
Vetoes block consensus
A diplomat said all seven candidates failed to win consensus after facing a veto from one of the permanent members, and the straw poll left none of the seven candidates approved by the five permanent members.
The same diplomat said the informal poll was the first time that Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States used colored straws to indicate vetoes, while the 10 elected members continued to use plain markers.
Mike Hammer refused to comment on U.S. media reports about opposition in Washington and said, “We have always said we simply want the best candidate.”
W. Nathalat said it is a sovereign right of countries “to nominate additional candidates if they wish,” after the poll opened the door to new nominations.
The straw poll framework required a candidate to secure support of 9 of the 15 Security Council members while also avoiding a veto from the five major powers, which the sources described as sharply divided.
Next steps and timelines
The sources said the next straw poll with red ballots will be held next week, and both Waltz and Russia’s U.N. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia left open the possibility of new candidates.
Waltz said, “We're going to get this done, I'm confident, before the end of the year,” while Nebenzia said, “That is my wish, definitely,” as the race continued without any candidate withdrawing.
The election rules described in the reporting required a candidate to receive support from at least nine members of the Council, five of whom are permanent, before the name goes to the General Assembly for final approval.
The sources also said António Guterres, who has led the United Nations for almost 10 years, will leave the post at the end of this year, and the second term is described as expiring on December 31, 2026.
The reporting framed the stakes as a choice of a successor for the UN secretary-general, with the job expected to return to a Latin American candidate and with pressure to pick a woman, while the permanent members remained divided.

UK, France, and Germany Gear Up for Ukraine Deployment With Major Military Drills in Poland
At least 1,500 troops from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland are expected to participate in military exercises in Poland in November, rehearsing the deployment of a multinational force to Ukraine following a potential ceasefire with Russia.

According to The Times on October 17, the exercises will focus on preparing European forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine as part of security arrangements intended to deter renewed Russian aggression.
The drills will test the movement of military personnel, coordination between national armed forces, and the delivery of essential supplies, including fuel and food. These logistical preparations are considered necessary for any future deployment of European troops to Ukrainian territory.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that thousands of military personnel would take part in the exercises next month. Streeting said the training would help participating countries prepare to support Ukraine’s military training requirements and post-war reconstruction.
The planned exercises form part of the Coalition of the Willing initiative, which brings together countries working on potential security guarantees for Ukraine following a cessation of hostilities.
According to The Times, the training will bring multinational units together to practice operating alongside one another, with particular attention to the practical requirements of moving and sustaining troops across borders.
The coalition’s plans have developed through a series of discussions between Ukraine and its European partners over the possible deployment of an international security contingent.
In January 2026, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and France signed a declaration of intent concerning the potential deployment of multinational forces following a peace agreement. The proposed mission would support Ukraine’s defense capabilities, military training, and long-term security.

articles.title: All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory on Trump’s team - The Guardian
articles.summary: All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory on Trump’s team  The GuardianTrump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations  BBCThe Global Story | America’s rogue ambassadors  BBCGreece’s President snubs Kimberly Guilfoyle of traditional honor as she leaves ambassador role  The IndependentTrump Donor Sues Kimberly Guilfoyle For Defamation After Allegations She Asked Him For $100,000  Forbes
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He has said so himself. But the president has often pointed to his hiring and promoting of women in an attempt to stave off criticism of both his policies and personal conduct over the years.
During his second term, however, there is one common characteristic among most of those who have departed the Trump administration.
In the space of just a few months, half of his eight high-level female officials have either resigned or been fired. All have been replaced by men. Several other women in his administration have also departed, whether voluntarily or involuntarily.
On Friday, Trump was forced to deny reports that he was considering replacing Susie Wiles, his White House chief of staff, and the first woman to do the job. “She’s gonna be here for a long time,” he claimed.
Numerous top male officials, meanwhile, from Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has on multiple occasions courted global condemnation, to the widely ridiculed FBI director Kash Patel, have survived intense scrutiny and repeated calls for their resignation – and yet remain in post.
Katie Zacharia
The latest female casualty was White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired on Friday just five days into the role. After a rocky start to her tenure, sparked by a widely panned first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. The ensuing semantics battle over whether or not she is a lawyer, or an attorney, placed her in a pickle – even with the rightwing cable network Fox News.
Zacharia had taken over from Karoline Leavitt, who said in August that she had chosen to resign from the role after 20 months so she could spend more time with her young family.
Kristi Noem
In terms of firings, the first domino to fall was former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, who was the face of Trump’s mass deportation campaign until she was unceremoniously sacked on 5 March. Her tenure was plagued by controversy, in large part amid national uproar over federal immigration enforcement operations that killed two US citizens in Minneapolis (one of whom Noem called a “domestic terrorist”, with no evidence), and coincided with a sharp decline in national support for Trump’s immigration agenda.
Her suggestion at a congressional hearing in March that Trump had known about her decision to approve a contract for a $220m ad campaign to encourage immigrants to “self-deport” – which prominently featured Noem on horseback – reportedly left Trump “pissed” and appeared to be the straw that broke the camel’s back. There had also been scrutiny of general leadership failures under Noem, as well as questions the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski, who also left his role when she was ousted.
Noem was repurposed as special envoy to the so-called “Shield of the Americas” coalition and, after that arrangement expired last month, is now serving in a vaguely defined advisory role. She was succeeded as DHS secretary by Markwayne Mullin.
Pam Bondi
Next fell former attorney general and Trump loyalist Pam Bondi, who was pushed out in April after a turbulent 14 months that saw the president increasingly frustrated over her mishandling of the Department of Justice’s long-awaited release of the Epstein files. The Epstein issue became a huge political liability for Trump and infuriated his Maga base, and he also felt that Bondi had failed to sufficiently prosecute his political enemies.
Bondi revealed a month after she was ousted that she had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Her deputy, Todd Blanche, assumed the role in August.
It’s worth noting that commerce secretary Howard Lutnick faced public scrutiny after details emerged surrounding his past ties to Jeffrey Epstein and visits to his private island. By contrast, the White House supported him after Democrats called for his resignation.
Lori Chavez-DeRemer
Also in April, former labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer stepped down after a Department of Labor inspector general investigation led to a series of allegations of misconduct, including having an affair with a subordinate and drinking alcohol on the job. She was replaced by Keith Sonderling.
Kash Patel has also been alleged to have been intoxicated or absent on the job. He has denied these allegations, and remains FBI director.
Tulsi Gabbard
A month later, in May, Tulsi Gabbard resigned from her position as Trump’s national intelligence director.
While she officially cited her husband’s rare cancer diagnosis, Gabbard was reportedly forced out after a tumultuous stint in which she was largely sidelined as Trump launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. She had previously testified to Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon.
Gabbard was replaced on an acting basis by Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no previous experience in the intelligence sphere, and eventually by Jay Clayton.
Kimberly Guilfoyle
Earlier this week, the Trump administration asked longtime Trump ally Kimberly Guilfoyle to step down from her position as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.
The only senior male official to have been somewhat punished by Trump since his return to office is Mike Waltz. The then-national security adviser was fired in May last year after inadvertently adding a journalist to a Signal group chat in which Pete Hegseth disclosed secret war plans.
Waltz had been on thin ice with Trump for a while, and the president was reportedly annoyed by Waltz’s hawkish stance on Iran. Signalgate merely sealed his fate.
But he didn’t disappear to some obscure advisory role; Waltz was nominated to the position of US ambassador to the United Nations. Hegseth, meanwhile, was allowed to ride out the controversy and – several controversies later, including allegations of war crimes – remains in post.
Democrats have highlighted the double standard that Trump only seems to fire women in his administration – even those who are ultra-loyal to him, and decidedly less incompetent than some of their male colleagues.
“If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic congresswoman, observed in April.
“I wouldn’t say I’m a feminist,” Trump said in a 2018 interview. “I mean, I think that would be, maybe, going too far. I’m for women. I’m for men. I’m for everyone.”
But not everyone gets to stick around.

articles.title: Nigeria seeks binding global rules on autonomous weapons, warns of terrorist threat - Peoples Gazette Nigeria
articles.summary: Nigeria seeks binding global rules on autonomous weapons, warns of terrorist threat  Peoples Gazette Nigeria
articles.full_text:
Nigeria has called for legally binding international rules governing autonomous weapons, warning that increasingly affordable military technologies could fall into the hands of terrorists.
The federal government made the appeal at the sixth plenary meeting of the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee, which is responsible for disarmament and international security.
Speaking in Nigeria’s national capacity, Deputy Permanent Representative Martin Adamu warned that technological advances were creating dangerous possibilities for armed groups and other non-state actors.
Mr Adamu said autonomous weapons were becoming increasingly accessible because of their relatively low cost, availability, and ease of replication.
He maintained that these developments could enable terrorist organisations to acquire sophisticated weapons capable of threatening international peace and security.
The representative consequently urged the international community to establish clear rules before the technologies became more widely available to armed groups.
Mr Adamu called for negotiations on a legally binding international instrument containing explicit prohibitions and regulations governing lethal autonomous weapons systems.
He stressed that meaningful human control must remain central to decisions involving the use of force and the taking of human life.
The envoy warned that weapons whose effects could not be sufficiently understood, predicted, or controlled raised serious legal, humanitarian, and security concerns.
He maintained that technological sophistication could never eliminate the responsibility of human beings for decisions made during military operations.
Mr Adamu urged the forthcoming Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons to provide the mandate required to commence negotiations.
The diplomat also expressed concern about the increasing integration of artificial intelligence into nuclear weapons systems.
He insisted that human judgment and control must be maintained in all decisions involving nuclear weapons, particularly as emerging technologies transform military capabilities.
The representative reaffirmed Nigeria’s conviction that the total elimination of nuclear weapons remained the only absolute guarantee against their use.
He expressed disappointment over the failure of the 11th Review Conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons to achieve a substantive outcome in May.
Mr Adamu called for transparent, verifiable, and irreversible measures towards nuclear disarmament, particularly by countries possessing nuclear weapons.
He also reaffirmed support for the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons and the African Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone Treaty, commonly known as the Treaty of Pelindaba.
Mr Adamu urged countries to support the early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty while respecting the right to peaceful nuclear energy.
In another significant announcement, Nigeria disclosed that it had submitted two draft resolutions addressing disarmament and illicit trafficking in small arms and light weapons on behalf of ECOWAS member states.
The delegation appealed to other UN member states to support the proposals, which reflect West Africa’s continuing concerns about weapons proliferation and insecurity.
Nigeria said its National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons was strengthening efforts to implement international and regional arms-control commitments.
The country also advocated stronger international cooperation against illicit arms diversion, trafficking, and emerging weapons technologies, while supporting UN-led cybersecurity cooperation and peaceful uses of outer space.

articles.title: US, Israel face threats of war if oil prices keep rising - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: US, Israel face threats of war if oil prices keep rising  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
High oil prices are going to be an issue over the next few weeks if they continue to stay above $100 a barrel. That is a clear challenge for the United States and also potentially for Israel in terms of keeping a lid on a renewed conflict with Iran prior to the elections in both countries.
It is no secret that the looming elections have shifted dynamics, expectations, and assessments of whether the conflict could restart.
The high oil prices come amid a decline in stock prices on Wall Street, amid concerns about AI companies and energy prices. That could tend to be a kind of triple threat affecting the United States, and thus also affecting Israel.
That is because the United States has been working hard to keep diesel and oil prices from skyrocketing. There has been a lot of messaging that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that other energy sources exist, but the question is whether the global market will accept those assertions.
Recent videos showing ships sinking in the Strait of Hormuz and all sorts of containers floating away as ships are in distress are certainly not something that will boost global optimism regarding supply chains, and it always remains a question whether enough ships are transporting energy supplies.
What will the Houthis do?
It also leads to questions about what the Houthis might do. The Houthis could try to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They could also encourage other Iranian proxies, such as those in Iraq, to continue attacks on Saudi oil and gas energy infrastructure.
A mysterious explosion in Iraq on Saturday appears to have struck an Iranian proxy group there. All this could continue to disrupt global trade. For example, when attacks hit pipelines or transit points in Saudi Arabia, repairs can take weeks. That creates disruption, and all those disruptions add up to the feeling in the global market that there is too much uncertainty.
This kind of uncertainty will affect the US. It already appears to be affecting policy regarding the Ukraine-Russia war, and this is the kind of thing that can lead to escalation in the Middle East or miscalculations in which something happens again with Iran.
Meanwhile, Iran continues to be blockaded, but it also tends to feel a bit confident about its next steps. As a result, we see potential for escalation within the next week or two.
Iran also knows there are elections in Israel and the United States; therefore, Iran and its proxies may want to take advantage of this period.

articles.title: Putin Brutally Mocked by His Own for Bogus War Briefing - The Daily Beast
articles.summary: Putin Brutally Mocked by His Own for Bogus War Briefing  The Daily BeastRussian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 15, 2026  Critical ThreatsThe Russia-Ukraine War Report Card, Oct. 14, 2026  Russia MattersISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 16, 2026  Kyiv PostPutin Claims 6,500 Square Kilometres Seized in Ukraine. The Reality Is 45 Times Smaller  UNITED24 Media
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin starred in a new Kremlin propaganda video Friday touting battlefield gains in Ukraine after being freshly fluffed by President Donald Trump’s show of support.
Footage circulated widely by the Kremlin and state-controlled media showed Putin visiting a command post of Russia’s Joint Group of Forces, where he was met by Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov.
The 74-year-old Russian leader showed up in military garb before walking into the command post, which oddly featured camouflage netting on the inside rather than the outside. Reading from papers in front of him, Putin rattled off a series of fantastical Russian “successes” on the battlefield since the start of the year.
He reported the seizure of 6,500 square kilometers of Ukrainian land by Russian forces, approximately 45 percent more than independent monitors have documented, or five times more than what the DeepState battlefield map reflects.
ADVERTISEMENT
Citing these “successes,” Putin went on to declare that “massive, coordinated strikes against Ukraine must continue.”
Gerasimov, in his performative briefing before the TV cameras, fed Putin a string of other demonstrably false claims about fresh gains on the battlefield. Nearly a year after first proudly reporting that Russian troops had taken control of the city of Kupyansk in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, Gerasimov did so again.
The claim was immediately debunked the first time it was made last November, and analysts say it’s still a lie; while small Russian assault groups have been making incursions into the city, it is not under Russian control, according to the Institute for the Study of War.
Gerasimov also claimed Russian troops have advanced to within three miles of Zaporizhzhia, despite an updated open-source intelligence map from DeepState placing the front line about 12 miles out.
The claims were quickly ridiculed even by pro-Kremlin military bloggers who are typically quick to celebrate Russian breakthroughs.
ADVERTISEMENT
“Trump will be just as impressed by the pace of the Russian Armed Forces’ advance as we are surprised by it now,” wrote one popular pro-Kremlin Telegram channel, Nash Regnum.
“I wonder if he can be prosecuted for spreading fake news about the Russian Armed Forces? This is an absolute disgrace!” wrote the pro-war channel Alex Parker Returns.
Others vented that there was “no point” trying to make sense of the claims.
“This has all been analyzed before. The relevant specialists—psychiatrists, addiction specialists, and gerontologists—will comment on what’s left,” wrote the pro-war blogger Artjockey.
Russia’s Defense Ministry has repeatedly been called out for fabricating battlefield gains and presenting a distorted view of the situation on the ground to Putin, but the disconnect has taken on a sharper focus as the Kremlin cites its purported military wins to bend the Trump administration in its favor in the hopes of forcing Ukraine to capitulate.
The Kremlin’s public announcements of (often dubious) battlefield breakthroughs have often coincided with major diplomatic talks, with similar claims made before Trump’s envoys visited Moscow and before Trump met with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky.
The latest publicity stunt comes as the Kremlin, having already won a partial easing of sanctions from Trump, reportedly works to have 260 billion euros ($292 billion) worth of assets unfrozen in Western countries.

articles.title: Any miscalculation by adversaries will invite response beyond their ‘imagination, calculation’, warns CNSC - Dawn
articles.summary: Any miscalculation by adversaries will invite response beyond their ‘imagination, calculation’, warns CNSC  Dawn
articles.full_text:
Commander National Strategic Command (CNSC) General Aamer Raza warned the country’s adversaries on Saturday that “any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or the calculation of the initiator”.
“To those who harbour hostile designs across our borders, our stance remains resolute and unambiguous. There is no space for conflict or war in a nuclearised environment and any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or calculation of the initiator,” warned the commander of Pakistan’s strategic command.
Addressing the passing-out parade of cadets of the 154th Long Course at the Pakistan Military Academy (PMA), Kakul, he reiterated that the country’s armed forces stood ready to “defend every inch of the motherland” at all costs.
The warning by the strategic command commander comes after provocative remarks by Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. He had warned Pakistan on Thursday that any “fresh terrorist activity from across the border would invite a strike even bigger than the last time”, according to Indian news agency ANI.
Gen Raza said that in the “post-truth era”, the country’s adversaries sought to drive a wedge between the people of Pakistan and its armed forces through “calculated disinformation and narrative warfare”.
He elaborated that following the failure of Operation Sindoor, the adversaries sought to “fracture Pakistan’s social cohesion and state infrastructure” through an escalation of proxy terrorism and sub-conventional warfare.
Gen Raza further said that hostile elements continue to attempt to exploit the country’s internal vulnerabilities to “cultivate proxy instruments against our national unity”.
“You must understand unequivocally that this conflict is waged directly against the security of our people and the freedom secured by the supreme sacrifices of our predecessors.”
The strategic command commander added that the people of Pakistan must remain acutely mindful that safeguarding the country’s unity, sovereign integrity and territorial inviolability is “an absolute imperative, which we shall uphold at all costs and under every circumstance”.
Addressing the newly-graduated cadets, he added that they must remain steadfast in their duty and unwavering in their resolve and “immune to malicious propaganda and narrative warfare”.
Pakistan’s role in regional peace
Gen Raza said the recent shifts in global geopolitics, particularly amid the escalating conflict in the Middle East, had “once again underscored Pakistan’s pivotal strategic importance on the international stage”.
“Our decisive role in restoring regional stability, exemplified by the landmark Islamabad Accord, demonstrates our enduring commitment to peace and diplomacy,” he said, adding that the Makkah Accord was “a sequel to the same vision of durable peace”.
Expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people, he said: “Our hearts remain heavily burdened by the ongoing tragedy in Palestine, where innocent men, women and children continue to endure unspeakable hardship and systematic oppression.”
He said the Pakistani nation stood “resolute and unwavering in its diplomatic, moral and political support” for the Palestinians.
“The persistent violence, targeting of non-combatants and destruction of civilian infrastructure are profound violations of international law and a grave stain on the collective conscience of humanity,” Gen Raza added.
“Today, the world witnesses increasing volatility, where grey-zone warfare and hybrid threats attempt to destabilise sovereign states,” he added.
FO condemns Singh’s ‘provocative remarks’
A day earlier, the Foreign Office (FO) condemned Singh’s “provocative remarks” threatening aggression against Pakistan, saying such statements highlighting the neighbouring country’s “hegemonistic mindset”.
“Pakistan rejects and condemns the Indian defence minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risk its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” FO spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said.
“We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a befitting response and reply to Indian aggression,” he said, referring to the brief military conflict between the two countries.
He said that there should be “no ambiguity” that Pakistan remained fully prepared to safeguard its “sovereignty and territorial integrity” against any “ill-advised aggression”.
Haider said Pakistan’s “restraint and commitment to peace” should not be mistaken for weakness, warning that any aggression would be met with a “forceful response”.
“India should draw an appropriate lesson from last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said.

articles.title: A socialist perspective to fight against war and austerity! Support the Socialist Equality Party in the Victorian election! - World Socialist Web Site
articles.summary: A socialist perspective to fight against war and austerity! Support the Socialist Equality Party in the Victorian election!  World Socialist Web Site
articles.full_text:
The Socialist Equality Party (SEP) is standing candidates in the November 28 Victorian election to provide workers and young people with a socialist and internationalist way forward against war, austerity, authoritarianism and the far right.
Our candidates are 31-year-old Morgan Peach, president of the SEP’s youth wing, the International Youth and Students for Social Equality, at the University of Melbourne, and Peter Byrne, a member of the Trotskyist movement for more than 40 years. They are standing on an independent ticket for the upper house region of Northern Metropolitan, which encompasses Melbourne’s industrial north and its diverse working-class communities.
This is a crisis election. It is taking place amid an already developing third world war, a deepening assault on democratic rights, a worsening cost-of-living disaster and sweeping attacks on the working class. There is mass hostility to Labor, the Coalition is fracturing, and the old parliamentary order is in crisis.
Under these conditions, the election is not a democratic contest, but a conspiracy by the political and media establishment. No other party will tell the truth about the decisive issues confronting workers and young people. Only the SEP explains that whichever party or combination of parties forms government, it will intensify the same militarist and pro-corporate agenda.
The fraud promoted by every other party is that the fundamental problems confronting workers can somehow be resolved within Victoria. The crises confronting workers in this state are expressions of the breakdown of global capitalism. They require the independent political mobilisation of the working class across Australia, as part of a unified international struggle against the profit system which leads to war and social misery.
Stop imperialist war! End AUKUS and the US alliance!
World War III’s opening shots have been fired, yet the election campaign is being conducted as if the gravest crisis confronting humanity does not exist. Labor, the Coalition, the Greens and One Nation are silent on the war because they are all pro-war parties.
Federally, the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is spearheading Australia’s role in the developing global war, with the Coalition’s support. Labor has aligned Australia ever more openly with Washington’s drive to offset its historic decline through military violence in the Middle East, against Russia and in the accelerating confrontation with China.
The US-Israeli war on Iran launched on February 28 marked a major turning point. It is an utterly criminal war of aggression involving the assassination of the leadership of a sovereign state and the murder of thousands of civilians, including school children, killed in the first days of the bombardment. It is inseparable from the ongoing Gaza genocide and the broader eruption of imperialist violence throughout the Middle East. Labor was among the first governments internationally to line up behind the assault, underscoring the complicity of Australian imperialism in war crimes expanding into a region-wide conflagration.
Pine Gap and the other joint facilities provide intelligence and targeting data essential to US operations. Labor deployed an Australian Wedgetail command-and-surveillance aircraft, missiles and military personnel to the Middle East. Australian personnel were aboard a US submarine that sank an Iranian vessel off the coast of Sri Lanka.
Imperialist barbarism in the Middle East is tied to the US-NATO proxy war in Ukraine, which is escalating to open warfare against Russia and, above all, the central strategic aim of US imperialism: preparations for war against nuclear-armed China. Under Albanese, Labor is completing Australia’s transformation into a launching pad for this catastrophe through the AUKUS military pact, expanded US basing and the conversion of northern Australia into a platform for American bombers, warships and marines.
Labor has lifted annual military expenditure to more than $60 billion and committed a further $53 billion over the coming decade. The $368 billion AUKUS submarine program, long-range missiles and new military infrastructure are preparations for a catastrophic war in the Indo-Pacific.
Every area of the country, including Victoria, is being integrated into the war drive.
The Victorian Labor government’s Defence Vision declares the state a “global defence and national security powerhouse.” More than 2,500 businesses are tied to the military supply chain, which receives $10.9 billion in annual Defence expenditure, while major universities are being drawn into military research, artificial intelligence, aerospace and autonomous weapons.
The drive to war abroad is accompanied by an escalating assault on democratic rights at home. In response to mass anti-war sentiment, the federal Labor government has spearheaded an offensive against opposition to the Gaza genocide, supported by state governments including Victorian Labor, which has introduced new restrictions on protests and expanded police powers.
These attacks have implications far beyond the suppression of opposition to the genocide. They are part of the strengthening of the repressive apparatus of the state in preparation for growing opposition to Australia's involvement in an expanding global war and the accompanying assault on workers' living standards.
- The SEP demands an immediate end to the assault on Iran and the Gaza genocide, an end to the US-NATO war against Russia and the dismantling of all preparations for war against China. Abolish AUKUS, end the US alliance, close the bases and dismantle the national-security apparatus directed against workers and anti-war opposition.
War is not the product of this or that bad government, nor of mistaken policies that can be corrected through parliamentary pressure. It arises from the capitalist profit system itself. Rival ruling classes compete for markets, resources and cheap labour, using their states and armed forces to secure profits at their rivals’ expense. That is why the struggle against war requires the building of an international anti-war movement of the working class fighting for world socialism.
Billions for social need—not the banks, big business and war!
War abroad means class war at home. Vast resources are being diverted into militarism and corporate handouts. At the same time, governments are demanding that workers pay for mounting state debts and the protection of corporate profits through cuts to public education, healthcare, housing and other essential services and wage suppression. Amid the worst cost-of-living crisis in decades, governments insist there is no money to meet the most basic social needs.
This escalating austerity offensive is at the heart of the Victorian election.
Victoria’s debt is forecast to rise from $175.6 billion in 2026–27 to $199.3 billion by 2029–30, with annual interest payments reaching $11.8 billion. These payments will build no school, treat no patient and house no family. They will flow to banks and financial institutions simply to service past borrowing.

Washington DC [US], October 17 (ANI): US President Donald Trump on Friday (local time) said he wanted the Russia-Ukraine war to end, claiming that both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wanted an end to the conflict, even as the Ukrainian leader accused Moscow of showing no genuine willingness to negotiate.
Speaking to reporters ahead of a rally in Georgia, Trump was asked whether he had forgotten that Putin started the war.
'Well, you know, I know the details, okay? And at some point, I'll release the details. But I don't care anything except for one. I want that war ended. 25,000 soldiers on average a month are being killed. Last month, it was 32,000 soldiers. And I think the two leaders, I deal with both of them. I think they want that war ended, too, and I think it's going to end. That's all I care about. I want that war to end,' Trump said.
However, Zelenskyy said Russia had shown no signs of readiness to end the conflict, accusing Putin of using rhetoric that did not reflect a genuine desire for peace.
Following a conversation with media representatives in Brussels, Zelenskyy said in a post on X, 'Putin doesn't want negotiations right now - in any format. He's playing word games, saying that "they're responding." It looks like a travesty of any genuine desire to end the war.'
The Ukrainian President also warned against easing sanctions on Russia, saying concessions over energy deals could lead to broader sanctions relief.
'We can't accept diesel deals, because gas deals will come next. I'm absolutely sure of that. After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things. It will eventually extend to the banking system, specific individuals, and the chemical industry. And there are risks around the frozen assets. If I don't defend that through diplomacy - who will do it for us?' he said.
Zelenskyy further accused Putin of seeking to undermine Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, questioning whether Russia's ambitions would be limited to eastern Ukraine.
'Putin wants to destroy us. He doesn't respect us, our sovereignty and territorial integrity. He really thinks that we are not a country, not a nation. Do you really believe that just the eastern part of our country will be enough for him? Then why did he go for Kyiv when the full-scale invasion began? Is that Donbas? No, it's the capital. Without the capital, there is no state,' he said.
He also warned that Russian drone activity posed a wider security risk to Europe, including NATO members, and cautioned against underestimating the threat.
'And what will happen afterwards? On what borders will he stay? If now he's testing all these drones against European, even NATO countries? They are not loud for now. They don't want to escalate because they have one Russian drone, two drones, ten. But you will be very loud when there will be ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and thousands of drones. We had one thousand drones yesterday,' Zelenskyy said.
Meanwhile, Putin praised Russian military strikes against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities and logistics centres, according to Russia's state-run TASS news agency.
During a visit to an auxiliary command post of the Joint Force on October 16, Putin claimed Russian forces were advancing along the frontline and had captured more than 1,300 square kilometres of territory in Donbas and Novorossiya in September.
'The Chief of the General Staff has already noted in his report that the military units have achieved a rapid pace of advance. As has already been mentioned here, in September alone, more than 1,300 square kilometers of territory in Donbass and Novorossiya have been liberated,' Putin said.
Putin also called for stronger air defence to protect civilian and military facilities, acknowledging that there was room to improve the effectiveness of Russian air defence crews.
'Overall, air defense combat crews are operating professionally. But, of course, there is room for improvement in this regard. We need to enhance the effectiveness of our defense of civilian, first and foremost civilian, and, of course, military facilities,' he said.
He ruled out discussing the establishment of a security zone along Russia's border territories during potential peace negotiations with Ukraine.
'Our task is to ensure absolute security of Russia's border territories in the future and we are not going to make this a subject of any potential peace talks with Ukraine,' Putin said.
The statements come amid continued hostilities and disagreements over negotiations, sanctions and the conditions for ending the war.
Earlier, Zelenskyy met European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to seek further European assistance for Ukraine's energy infrastructure, air defence and financial resilience.

Trump had announced the immediate energy ceasefire on October 11, calling on both sides to stop targeting energy infrastructure.
The arrangement came under strain after Zelenskyy accused Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities, which he said had damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted electricity supplies. (ANI)

articles.title: Super El Nino 'grows second arm' after Brits issued 'stock up' warning - AOL.com
articles.summary: Super El Nino 'grows second arm' after Brits issued 'stock up' warning  AOL.comSuper El Niño breaks sea temperature record weeks ahead of expected peak  BBCNASA satellites observe historic 2026 El Niño  Phys.orgA super El Niño winter is coming and the first official forecast is in  CNNA record-breaking El Niño is still developing – likely bringing a cold winter to the UK  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
A striking new set of weather maps shows the ongoing 'Super El Niño' event appears to have developed a second extension, suggesting a significant expansion of the unusually warm waters across the Pacific Ocean. Images released by Peru's National Meteorological and Hydrological Service (Senamhi) show the warm-water anomaly spreading beyond its previous footprint over recent weeks. A map published on September 30 depicted a broad ribbon of elevated sea-surface temperatures stretching westward from the coasts of Ecuador and Peru.
However, updated data collected on October 14 paints a different picture. The latest image suggests the warm waters have extended further south along the Chilean coastline and into the south-eastern Pacific.
The expansion has created what looks like a second arm emerging from the main body of warm water, giving the phenomenon an increasingly pronounced and unusual shape. It means a far larger area of the eastern Pacific is now being affected by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures, with some regions recording temperatures more than 3C above the seasonal average, reports Mail Online.
The development is likely to intensify concerns among climate experts, who have warned that the current El Niño is strengthening rapidly. The growing expanse of warm water adds to evidence suggesting the phenomenon could develop into one of the most powerful El Niño events seen in centuries, with the potential to influence weather patterns around the world.
Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather told the publication: "I think that this year's El Niño event is likely to be the strongest in 1,000 years if the latest models of its peak prove accurate." Britons have already been advised to brace for a turbulent autumn marked by heavy rainfall and storms, before colder and more settled conditions take hold during the winter months. The warning comes as government officials have encouraged households to make basic preparations for periods of severe weather.
Last month, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs urged people to ensure they have essential supplies available in case extreme conditions disrupt access to services. The department said that maintaining a small reserve of food could prove beneficial during emergencies, reducing reliance on immediate assistance if adverse weather affects local infrastructure or transport links.
Dr Chloe Brimicombe, a climate researcher at the University of Oxford, said colder, calmer weather can also create challenges for Britain's renewable energy supply.
"Wind power generates 40 per cent or more of the UK's electricity during winter and cold, calm periods can require more gas power to make up for lower wind generation and increased demand for heating," she wrote on The Conversation.
El Niño is one phase of the naturally recurring El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate pattern that alternates between warmer and cooler conditions every two to seven years.
During an El Niño event, the trade winds that typically push warm surface waters westward across the Pacific towards Australia weaken significantly or, in some cases, reverse direction altogether. As a result, warm water accumulates across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, particularly off the western coast of South America.
US meteorologist Ryan Maue wrote on X: "New maps show Earth almost entirely in the red. El Niño continues at 'maximum power' into the winter with planetary heating dialled up everywhere except the United States."
The latest alert follows the release of dramatic weather maps by meteorologists, showing vast regions of the planet highlighted in red, a sign that temperatures are increasingly likely to rise above seasonal norms.
The striking forecasts point to widespread warmth across multiple continents, reinforcing concerns that global temperatures could remain exceptionally high as the powerful El Niño pattern continues to strengthen.

Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.
Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.
The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.
Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.
Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.
“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”
Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.
“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said.
Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.
Since 27 September, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.
Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.
“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”
On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that America wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers. “We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing,” Rubio said. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff.”
Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military coordination.
Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions and international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named.
“Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.
A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the international criminal court to intervene.
Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections to be held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin claimed that Moscow’s forces had captured approximately 6,500 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory and 310 settlements since the beginning of 2026. However, independent battlefield assessments suggest Russia’s actual territorial gains are roughly 45 times smaller than the Kremlin’s claims.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) in its October 16 assessment, Putin and Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov significantly overstated Russian advances across several frontline regions, including Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia.
ISW estimates that Russia achieved a net territorial gain of approximately 144.5 square kilometers between January and September 2026. Russian forces also experienced periods of territorial losses, including a net loss of approximately 122 square kilometers since September 1.
Gerasimov separately claimed that Russian troops had captured more than 1,800 square kilometers and 92 settlements since September. ISW’s findings contradict those figures, indicating that Ukrainian counterattacks have reversed Russian advances in several sectors.
In Donetsk region, Putin claimed that Ukrainian forces controlled only around 10% of the territory. ISW instead estimates that Ukraine retains approximately 5,530 square kilometers, representing more than 20% of the region.
The institute also found no evidence supporting Russian claims of capturing Dobropillia or entering Druzhkivka. Russian forces remain at least 12 kilometers from Druzhkivka and nine kilometers from Kramatorsk, according to the assessment.
Similar discrepancies were identified in Zaporizhzhia region. While Putin claimed Ukraine controlled just 16.5% of the region, ISW assessed Ukrainian control at approximately 24.6%.
Gerasimov also claimed Russian forces were within five kilometers of Zaporizhzhia city. ISW placed their positions at least 20.95 kilometers away, or approximately 11.6 kilometers when accounting for limited Russian infiltration attempts.
In Sumy region, Russian commanders reported capturing more than 300 square kilometers during the summer and autumn. ISW estimated Russian territorial gains in the region at just 99.1 square kilometers since the beginning of 2026.
ISW assessed that the Kremlin’s exaggerated battlefield claims form part of a broader information campaign intended to portray Russian advances as inevitable and pressure Ukraine and its Western partners into accepting Moscow’s negotiating demands.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starlink systems were part of a “planned operation” aimed at undermining the country’s defences.
The Ukrainian leader’s latest comments come amid the sharpest deterioration in relations with US President Donald Trump since their explosive Oval Office meeting in February 2025, and as Moscow escalates its air war against Kyiv ahead of winter.
On Friday night, Trump refrained from imposing additional sanctions on Russia that were mandated by a sweeping law passed by Congress.
In a message to reporters over WhatsApp on Saturday, Zelenskyy said that Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian drone units worked at high speeds in the EU — up to 180kph — but cut out inside Ukraine when they flew faster than 160kph.
The maximum speed for Ukrainian drones equipped with Starlink systems was 161kph, he said, adding that “exceeding this limit causes the Starlink connection to cut out completely, resulting in the loss of the drone”.
He said Ukraine had conducted the tests to determine whether SpaceX was facing technical issues, as Kyiv had been told by Washington, or if the restrictions were a “planned operation . . . to restrict us, cut us off and prevent us from defending ourselves and protecting our people, both at the front and among the civilian population”.
Ukraine “sent a couple of vehicles equipped with Starlink terminals into European Union territory”, he said, without naming the countries where the tests were conducted.
“They moved at speeds exceeding 180kph, and the Starlink systems worked perfectly. We have the relevant logs and evidence to prove this,” he said.
“The conclusion is clear: the restrictions are in effect within Ukraine but do not apply within the European Union. In other words, this is a planned operation.”
Kyiv was blindsided by unexplained intelligence lapses from foreign partners about Russian ballistic missile strikes over the weekend, according to officials, which was followed by the surprise restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet systems used by Ukraine’s military, particularly its drone units.
Ukrainian troops said they had been forced to suspend operations owing to the speed limits placed on the systems, which made them vulnerable to Russian air defences. Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the drone interceptors that Ukraine relies on to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones had also been hobbled.
He said Ukraine was increasingly relying on its fighter jets to intercept drones, with a success rate of more than 50 per cent.
Musk, who controls SpaceX, shifted any blame for the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield — the military-grade version of the system — to the Trump administration, noting that they were owned and controlled by the US government. He said any limits on speed or usage would have been decided by the Pentagon or the president.
Trump said on Friday that neither he nor Musk were responsible for the Starlink restrictions.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio reiterated that line to reporters on Saturday night. “No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” Rubio said. “But my understanding is it’s back up and running.”
A bipartisan group of senators on Thursday demanded the Pentagon open an investigation into the matter.
The intelligence gaps and the alleged throttling of Starlink came right before Trump waived new sanctions on Moscow.
Zelenskyy had praised the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which was signed by Trump last month, as a “major victory”. But on Saturday, he said “the lifting of sanctions will continue, unfortunately”. Zelenskyy added that Trump’s decision to exempt Russia “only helps the Russians”.
“It certainly doesn’t stop the war,” he said.
Last week, Trump also agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin to “immediately” release 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel to US and global markets ahead of midterm elections next month.
Zelenskyy also discussed with European countries information that Russia would attempt to reclaim frozen assets “through some partners”.
“But as of today the situation is under control,” the Ukrainian president said.
Kyiv was also surprised by Trump’s announcement last Sunday that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”.
